item.title: Trump Endorses Netanyahu as Best U.S. Partner in Tight Israeli Election
item.description:
President Trump endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel on Sunday, giving the embattled Israeli leader a boost nine days before a hard-fought parliamentary election.

In a lengthy post on Truth Social, Mr. Trump wrote a message to the “Great People of Israel” contending that anyone other than Mr. Netanyahu would be the “wrong Leader.”

“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” he wrote. “Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”

Relations between Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu have become increasingly tense, particularly over the nations’ joint war against Iran. But in his endorsement Mr. Trump called Mr. Netanyahu a “Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, thanked the president for his “amazing support and work together.”

“Together, we’ll finish the job,” Mr. Netanyahu wrote on social media.

Israelis are set to head to the polls on Oct. 27 in an election that is widely seen as a referendum on Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership. Many in Israel fault Mr. Netanyahu for failing to prevent Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and steering Israel to near-unprecedented diplomatic isolation during the subsequent war in Gaza. Nonetheless, Mr. Netanyahu and his allies are neck and neck with their opponents in polling.

While the tenor of the relationship between Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Trump has varied wildly over the years, Mr. Netanyahu often highlighted his influence over the U.S. president in his pitch to voters. Ahead of a 2019 election, Mr. Netanyahu featured pictures of himself shaking hands with Mr. Trump in massive billboards across the country. The two leaders worked closely ahead of the decision to launch a joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, including a February visit by Mr. Netanyahu to the White House.

But the relationship soured considerably as the war with Iran stretched into a grueling slog that ensnarled the global economy. Mr. Trump appeared to have increasingly little patience for the conflict, moving to secure cease-fires with Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon over Israeli objections. The president later admitted that he had privately called Mr. Netanyahu “crazy” over Israeli actions in Lebanon.

Mr. Trump’s endorsement will likely carry some credence for Israelis, though perhaps not as much as it once did. Many Israelis hail Mr. Trump for securing the release of the remaining Israeli hostages in Gaza last year when his team helped broker a fragile cease-fire with Hamas. But others now view him as an unpredictable leader who dropped the ball in the middle of the war with Iran, which Israel had hoped to continue prosecuting.

item.title: Trump Outlines Rapid Plan to Close and Overhaul D.C. Golf Course
item.description:
President Trump said on Sunday that his administration had finalized plans to transform East Potomac Golf Links in Washington into a “World Class Championship Golf Course,” saying the municipal course would close within four weeks and that its replacement would be playable in about 15 months.

The announcement set up another frantic legal clash over the site. A federal judge ordered the administration in July to present her with any long-term plans for the course and not to carry out a surprise overhaul as the president had with the East Wing of the White House and the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The Interior Department appeared to have done just that earlier this month, taking down hundreds of trees over a holiday weekend and giving the court and a group suing to stop any changes to the course less than a day to react.

In a post on social media on Sunday morning, Mr. Trump appeared to affirm what a historical-preservation group and two Washington residents had warned of in a federal lawsuit: that the administration might move to seize the existing course before they had a real chance to oppose the plan.

Mr. Trump wrote that he had already notified professional golf organizations that “they will soon have one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World to put on their list of great places to play, and hold Major Events.” He added that he had secured a design by Tom Fazio, a well-known designer who has planned other courses owned by the Trump Organization.

The president shared a rendering of the planned course that resembled a blurred-out image sitting on his desk in a photo shared on Friday by Katie Zacharia, his press secretary who was ousted from the role after less than a week.

In response to the post, Judge Ana C. Reyes, who has presided over the case, ordered the Justice Department to reconcile the announcement with what had been said in court by Sunday at 8 p.m.

She noted that the government had consistently denied that any decisions on the future of the course had been made along the lines of the vision Mr. Trump has shared publicly. She quoted a Justice Department lawyer who, as recently as Friday, said that Mr. Trump “at most” had given only “preliminary thought to” the future of the course.

The group opposing the plan has argued that the existing course provided an affordable and accessible option to players in the Washington area who would be harmed by its conversion into a more exclusive, professional-level destination. Critics and local golfers have also expressed doubt that the isolated Hains Point peninsula, where the course is situated, could handle the traffic that professional tournaments would demand.

The map Mr. Trump shared on Sunday showed the new course covering the bulk of East Potomac Park, with the proposed 12th hole situated over what is now a public picnic area and playground at Hains Point. In addition to the current municipal course, the perimeter of the island is also a popular cycling circuit.

“East Potomac Park is a national park, golf course and recreational facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy,” said Skye Perryman, the president of Democracy Forward, which is representing the group challenging the plan. “Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves.”

Mr. Trump has signaled for months that he intended to realize the plan, and he was photographed touring the site and studying blueprints with Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Mr. Fazio in June.

But because there had not previously been imminent plans to move forward with the redevelopment, Judge Reyes was hesitant for months to preemptively block the Trump administration from making any changes to the existing course. Instead, she had prevailed upon the Justice Department to notify her before making any major changes.

During a hearing in July, a Justice Department lawyer said that no decision had been reached on the fate of the course.

After it was revealed that the Interior Department cleared hundreds of trees last weekend, Judge Reyes excoriated the Justice Department for failing to keep her apprised during a fiery hearing on Monday. She accused the government of “double speak” for representing in court that the work was planned maintenance, despite Mr. Trump’s public vision to transform the course.

Seething at a government lawyer, Judge Reyes turned an extended portion of the four-hour hearing into an effort to identify who had given the go-ahead to begin the work. She ordered the government to track down several senior officials in the Interior Department to testify on the spot but was able to reach only one.

Judge Reyes lamented that she had tried to avoid “playing parks and rec” or policing landscaping decisions at the course. But confronted with signs that the administration was rushing forward, she ordered the government not to remove any more trees until Oct. 26 to give the group opposing the plan time to respond.

The question of who authorized the work is expected to be the focus of a hearing on Monday, at which Judge Reyes had ordered Gregory Wischer, a Trump appointee at the Interior Department, and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify.

But the Justice Department escalated the standoff on Friday and filed a motion to disqualify Judge Reyes, citing her frustration at the hearing in order to question her impartiality and ask that she recuse herself from the case. She ordered both sides to file a response to the request by Sunday afternoon.

On Sunday, Judge Reyes also ordered Stanley Woodward Jr., the associate attorney general who filed the motion to disqualify her, to attend the hearing on Monday in which more senior Interior Department officials are scheduled to testify.

In the post on Sunday, Mr. Trump repeated an argument the government had made in court that clearing trees from the course was meant to return it to its original 1920s design, which featured open sight lines. But while the government indicated last week that the tree removal was proposed in a seven-year-old historic-restoration concept, Mr. Trump appeared to suggest that it was linked to the “Fazio Design” that he said would be built starting on Nov. 15.

item.title: Semi-Truck Rollover Spills Dozens of Cattle Across Downtown Kansas City
item.description:
A tractor-trailer carrying about 120 head of cattle through Kansas City, Mo., collided with a car early Sunday, fell off an interstate-highway overpass onto another car and spilled out dozens of animals, officials said. Some roamed through downtown in the pre-dawn hours.

The crash occurred shortly before 3 a.m. on the westbound Interstate 70 curve over the southbound lanes of Interstate 35, according to patrol officers who discovered it. The lower highway remained closed through the early afternoon, the police said.

The truck driver and the driver of the car that was on the lower road were reported to be in stable condition on Sunday afternoon, said Michael Hopkins, a battalion chief with the Kansas City, Mo., fire department.

The impact of the crash tore open the multilevel livestock trailer, filled with young cattle, killing 45 to 60 instantly and trapping others, said Sgt. Phil DiMartino of the Kansas City, Mo., police department.

Dozens of surviving cattle escaped onto the highway and wandered into surrounding neighborhoods. By midmorning, sightings were reported as far away as Kansas City, Kan., across the Kansas River.

The escaped cows caused other crashes on the streets, Sergeant DiMartino said, and more calls to the police, he said.

Officials called livestock handlers, some of whom rode horseback, to help wrangle the roaming cattle. All the livestock were found by the early afternoon, Sergeant DiMartino said, with the aid of drones.

item.title: Driver Whose Truck Plowed Onto Soccer Field, Killing Two, Is Released
item.description:
The driver whose truck plowed onto a soccer field in Kansas, leaving two people dead and 10 others injured, has been released without charges pending the results of toxicology testing, the police said.

The Wichita Police Department has not shared the name of the 34-year-old woman but said that she was drug tested and that the authorities also conducted a mechanical examination of her black Chevrolet pickup.

The two people who died at the Stryker Sports Complex were identified on Sunday as Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson, Kan.

The woman appears to have been parked in a parking space near the soccer fields before the truck drove onto the field, the Wichita Police Department said, citing a preliminary investigation. Two children were inside the truck with her, and another one of her children was playing soccer on another field at the complex, the police said.

The truck struck 10 others who were taken to nearby hospitals. The victims ranged in age from 5 to 68, the police said.

The injured were a 5-year-old girl, a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-old boys, a 9-year-old girl, a 28-year-old woman, a 32-year-old man, a 59-year-old woman, a 65-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man. Another person, a 61-year-old woman, was taken to the hospital with a separate medical issue, the police said.

Investigators interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the woman and the children in the truck with her, before consulting with the Sedgwick County District Attorney’s Office, the news release said.

Teams from the Sporting Wichita Academy, a soccer club league for all ages, were playing on Saturday at the complex, which has 11 fields that host different sporting events and a 112,000-square-foot indoor facility.

The games drew families from across the state, with some driving multiple hours for their children’s games.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

Lauren Hard, Orlando Mayorquín and Ishani Desai contributed reporting. Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: On the Campaign Trail, Trump Tries to Outrun a Bad Week in Washington
item.description:
President Trump continued to sell himself as the Republican Party’s savior as he crisscrossed the country in recent days, making it clear in words and sheer presence that this midterm election is about him.

But back in the nation’s capital, Mr. Trump’s White House was consumed by dramas that reinforced why polls show that his presidency itself has become a drag on Republican tickets.

On Monday, Mr. Trump asked for the resignation of Kimberly Guilfoyle, his ambassador to Greece, after a string of embarrassing reports, including that she urged a donor to pay for her $100,000 credit card debt. The president on Thursday canceled the Pentagon’s planned livestream of an execution of the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting after bipartisan outrage. And on Friday, he ousted his press secretary of five days after her bumpy debut.

Meantime, the White House Counsel’s Office was investigating a dispute between two prominent Trump allies and former administration officials over claims one of them misallocated funds for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, a heated conflict stemming from a transaction from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company. And the administration deepened its standoff with the federal judge presiding over a lawsuit challenging the president’s plan for a golf course, pushing to disqualify her after she excoriated federal officials for ripping up hundreds of mature trees with little notice.

Together, the string of controversies invoked the chaos of Mr. Trump’s first term, when infighting among his aides regularly burst into public view. The week also encapsulated how Mr. Trump’s approval ratings have been dragged down by his administration’s policies and allegations of self-dealing that have shadowed much of his inner circle.

“It feels like late 2020,” said Alyssa Farah Griffin, who served in Mr. Trump’s White House during his first term. “There’s almost too much chaos. It's drinking from the fire hose, and you can’t anticipate the next plot twist from this administration.”

She added: “You couldn’t dream up a worse week for the White House heading into the midterms.”

Mr. Trump's approval rating sits around 37 percent, the lowest of his presidency, according to The New York Times average of polls. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll conducted Oct. 9-13 and released on Sunday shows his approval among Republicans dropped from 88 percent near the start of his term to 79 percent. The survey also found, for the first time in a decade, that voters trust Democrats more on the economy, and 66 percent of voters said Mr. Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself.

A Fox News poll from this month found that government corruption ranked first among voters’ concerns, followed by inflation, gas prices, government leadership and health care. Democrats are making the case that corruption is in fact a cause of higher prices.

“To the extent that Republicans are successful in keeping the Senate, it will be because of their success in distancing themselves from some of the president’s policies,” former Senator Jeff Flake, Republican of Arizona and longtime Trump critic who served as ambassador to Turkey in the Biden administration, said in an interview. “And that’s not a position you want to be in. And it’s not just the policies. It’s the weirdness of it. The crass and crude and vulgar language. It’s awful. It doesn’t help Republicans.”

On the road, Mr. Trump made no mention of the latest controversies. He held rallies in six different states, stretching from Alaska to Georgia, serving up a familiar message: His presidency has been an unbridled success, and Democratic victories next month threaten America’s future.

Inside the cosseted bubble of a Trump rally, composed largely of MAGA superfans, that message was met with hearty concurrence from the president’s adoring fans.

Tara Green, a front desk office administrator who attended the rally in Wasilla, Alaska, said seeing Mr. Trump was “an opportunity of a lifetime.”

“Trump has a vision, and it might take time, but it is fixing things,” she said. “I have every belief and trust in him.”

Still, there were signs of Mr. Trump’s eroding support, even inside his bubble. The president was interrupted by protesters at each of his rallies, once a rare occurrence. And swaths of the arenas, which Mr. Trump used to pack with ease, remained empty.

At a check-in desk for special guests on Saturday outside Truist Arena in Highland Heights, Ky., one volunteer asked a staffer for Mr. Trump how many people they were expecting at the rally. The staffer, outfitted in a “Team Trump” jacket, said they had expected a larger audience than was on hand. (The entire upper level of the arena remained empty during the rally.) The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Trump’s closing message also was notably meandering, even for a man who boasts about “the weave,” his description of how he bounces from one topic to another without any discernible connection.

The president kicked off most rallies this week by praising the appearance of Republican male candidates. (He seemed particularly enthralled by the backside of Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, bringing it up at two different rallies this week.)

He recounted his own political successes and margins of victory in the states he was visiting, most of which are historically Republican strongholds and a sign of how much ground his party is defending this year.

And he reminded voters of the basket of incentives he’s offering if they elect Republicans, expanding it from cash bonuses to pardons and investments from the Pentagon.

But even the president downplayed the impact of his signature midterm giveaway: a controversial promise to give $5,000 for every American adult — which he calls the “Trump dividend” — if Republicans retain control of Congress.

Describing a hypothetical conversation about a couple looking to spend the money, “Let’s go to Palm Beach and join the president for lunch. Let’s have lunch at Mar-a-Lago, where for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert,” he said, with a laugh. “I shouldn’t say that.”

That line in particular underscored how Mr. Trump has repeatedly seemed to minimize voter anxieties about rising costs, one reason Republicans have tried distancing themselves from the president.

Even among rally-goers, there seemed more wariness than in earlier elections, and loyalty to Mr. Trump seemed more important than concerns about policy or the turbulence in his administration.

Ustun Yuksel, a Trump supporter who has a Ph.D in political science and lives in Dawsonville, Ga., acknowledged that he needs to work on addressing cost of living issues.

“They can definitely do better,” he said, while waiting for Mr. Trump in Dalton, Ga.

But he said he likes Mr. Trump’s foreign policy. And he had no interest in discussing the latest headlines out of the White House.

“I don’t want to talk about it,” Mr. Yuksel said just after the news broke that Katie Zacharia, the White House press secretary, was ousted. “I don’t want to say anything.”

A few hours later, as Amy Thomas, a bail bonds agent from Cleveland, Tenn., waited in traffic to exit the rally, she jumped out of her car to capture Mr. Trump depart on Marine One. She said Mr. Trump was “getting the job done” and demurred when asked about the turmoil in the administration.

“My friend follows it more than I do,” she said of the firings and latest drama.

item.title: Migrants From Ukraine and Sudan to Keep Deportation Protections for Now
item.description:
The Trump administration said on Sunday that people from Ukraine and Sudan would be able to keep their temporary humanitarian protections for now, allowing them to continue living in the United States.

Temporary Protected Status, a program meant to help foreign nationals who cannot safely return home because of armed conflict or natural disasters in their countries, was set to expire for about 100,000 Ukrainians and about 1,800 Sudanese on Monday.

The Homeland Security Department said that an announcement on the future of both programs would be “made at the appropriate time” and that people covered by them would be protected until then. But the department did not provide more information on the timing of the announcement.

Ukraine is nearly five years into a war that has battered the country, and civilian casualties have hit the highest levels since the beginning of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Sudan is in the middle of a devastating civil war that has engulfed the country for more than three years, leading to a severe food crisis.

The decision to hold off making an announcement mirrored a similar move by the Trump administration last month to allow people from El Salvador to keep their deportation protections for now. Since then, no announcement has been made and more than 170,000 Salvadorans have been left in limbo.

The moves notably diverge from the Trump administration’s previous attempts to swiftly dismantle T.P.S. programs as part of its broader campaign to restrict immigration, ending the protections for 13 of the 17 countries once covered. They also sharply differ from the administration’s treatment of about 350,000 Haitians who lost their temporary deportation protections this summer, despite ongoing unrest in their country. In a barrage of social media posts, homeland security officials cheered on deportation flights to Haiti.

But President Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown has become a political problem for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections on Nov. 3, and his party is at risk of losing control of one or both chambers of Congress. The decision to keep the protections for Ukrainians also comes as tensions between Mr. Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine have erupted over Mr. Trump’s thawing relationship and deal-making with Moscow, raising questions about the future of U.S. support for Ukraine.

This month, the United States lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports that were first put in place to limit Moscow’s ability to finance the war. On Friday, Mr. Trump signed an order exempting Russia from new sanctions approved by Congress that were intended to target Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions.

Mr. Trump’s efforts stem from concerns that high fuel prices could hurt Republicans in the midterms. He has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries so that Moscow can send more diesel to global markets. But Mr. Zelensky said last week that he would resume the strikes after Russia refused to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, defying Mr. Trump.

The Trump administration’s decision to keep the deportation protections, at least for now, is a sign that the United States is still committed to providing some assistance for Ukrainians.

Kate, a recent high school graduate in Nebraska, said she was glad that T.P.S. would not immediately end for Ukrainians. She said that she fled the country with her mother and brother four years ago, and that the program had allowed them to live in the United States.

But Kate, who agreed to be interviewed on the condition that only her first name be used because she fears being targeted by immigration agents, said she worried that the United States could still terminate the protections before the war ended.

She recalled living in a bomb shelter shortly after the war broke out and frequently hearing rockets fly over her hometown. “I’m very scared to go back,” she said. “Nobody’s safe there.”

The administration’s decision to hold off making an announcement about the programs was also criticized by some former homeland security officials who said the moves created uncertainty for families and employers across the country.

“In light of the armed conflicts that continue in Ukraine and Sudan, extending T.P.S. is the right decision,” said Royce Murray, an assistant secretary at the Homeland Security Department during the Biden administration. “But the lack of clarity about the decision — including for how long T.P.S. will last — creates incredible instability for T.P.S. holders and the employers who rely on them.”

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

item.title: The 2028 Presidential ‘Shadow Primary’ Descends on the Midterms
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom of California spent his Saturday weaving through New Hampshire, campaigning with midterm candidates as he faced questions about his presidential ambitions. Next weekend, former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is weighing another White House bid, plans to be in the state with the Democratic Senate nominee. And days after that, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, who is also considering a run, will appear there, too.

In the final stage of this year’s midterms, prospective presidential candidates are parachuting into battleground states to rally support for candidates on the ballot this fall, road-test their stump speeches, and introduce themselves to voters and activists. The Democratic schedule is especially packed in New Hampshire, an early presidential nominating state where there is a competitive Senate race. While New Hampshire has lost its long vaunted first-in-the-nation Democratic primary status to South Carolina, it will go third in 2028.

“Got here last night from the most un-Trump state in the United States of America, California,” Mr. Newsom told the crowd in Exeter, N.H., at a rally on Saturday with Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate nominee, as well as other Democratic candidates. His 10-minute speech focused primarily on Mr. Trump.

Ambitious Republicans, too, are trying to leave lasting marks across the country in this year’s high-stakes elections. Vice President JD Vance and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas are hitting the road for midterm candidates, including in states expected to figure prominently in the next G.O.P. presidential race.

In both parties, the possible presidential candidates’ itineraries reflect their standings, showing where they are in demand and where they are not. At times, midterm candidates have subtly or loudly distanced themselves from some of them.

In other cases, midterm contenders have welcomed the extra attention and support. Mr. Newsom’s trip to New Hampshire follows recent visits by Senator Raphael Warnock, Democrat of Georgia, and Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, among others. Mr. Pappas, whose roster of surrogates from outside New Hampshire has grown, is facing former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican.

“I think of political campaigns like building a house. You have to build the foundation first before building the walls. That’s what these visits are,” said Jim Demers, a veteran New Hampshire Democratic strategist, who like other operatives refers to the current phase as the “shadow primary.”

At the town hall event in Exeter, Mr. Newsom popped out from behind a curtain, beaming as Macklemore and Ryan Lewis’s “Can’t Hold Us” played in the background. Asked about his political future, he waved his hand and said, “It’s all about 2026.”

While others similarly say they are solely focused on this year’s elections, Democratic and Republican strategists see multiple purposes in these visits.

“A campaign for president is like having an endoscopy and a colonoscopy at the same time,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “A lot of candidates are truly deciding whether they want to do this.”

Midterm travel may be especially attractive to lesser-known politicians looking to raise their national profiles, and to those who don’t hold public office.

Mr. Buttigieg, who left his post in the Biden administration in early 2025, has endorsed more than 100 candidates this cycle and campaigned for them in more than 30 states. Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky has headlined Democratic Party dinners or conventions in nine states, including several that will hold early presidential primaries. Representative Ro Khanna of California has campaigned for more than 70 candidates.

Others have been more selective with their travels. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, recently campaigned in Michigan, another early-nominating state, with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate. She plans to appear in Maine this week with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee there.

The country faces a “pivotal and consequential moment,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said in Michigan on Friday. She brushed aside speculation about her 2028 plans, saying, “What matters right now is the next 19 days.”

Ms. Harris also recently appeared with Dr. El-Sayed. She plans to visit Nevada, an early-nominating state, as well as Mississippi, Georgia and Wisconsin.

But Senate candidates in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas have publicly and pre-emptively uninvited Ms. Harris, whose ties to the Biden administration have made her unwelcome in some conservative-leaning states.

Tensions have flared in other ways. In recent weeks, Latino leaders became angry that the Democratic Governors Association, chaired by Mr. Beshear, was not investing more money into Gina Hinojosa’s race for Texas governor against Greg Abbott, the Republican incumbent. They made veiled threats to withhold their support from Mr. Beshear should he run for president in 2028.

Within a week, the D.G.A. made a seven-figure donation to help elect Ms. Hinojosa.

Some potential presidential candidates have sought to balance their own re-elections: Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania are on the ballot in November. Mr. Shapiro recently started a federal political-action committee that enables him to give money to congressional candidates.

On the Republican side, Mr. Vance has campaigned in Kansas, Michigan and other battlegrounds. In Michigan on Thursday, he called the Senate contest “the most important race in the United States of America,” as he stumped for Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee.

Mr. Trump’s sinking approval ratings have made the president and, by extension, Mr. Vance a liability for some battleground candidates, as they seek to energize the party’s base voters. When Mr. Vance held a rally in Iowa last month, Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, didn’t attend, citing scheduling conflicts.

Republican “candidates in swing seats want his voters, not necessarily his baggage,” said Matt Klink, a Republican strategist in California, speaking of Mr. Trump.

Mr. Cruz, who has clashed publicly with Mr. Vance, has raised money and campaigned in his home state of Texas for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in a tight contest, and visited Iowa, which has been an early Republican nominating state, among other places.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a frequent target in Democrats’ campaign attacks, has also campaigned for Republicans this cycle in Iowa and Kentucky, a departure from past Pentagon officials who have stayed out of politics.

In New Hampshire, Derek Thibeault, 55, the chair of the Nashua Democratic City Committee, said he approached Mr. Newsom at an event on Saturday and asked the governor to let him know when he’d be back to campaign for the White House.

“He gave me a big laugh, but he didn’t say no,” Mr. Thibeault said.

Andrew Sylvia contributed reporting from New Hampshire.

item.title: Key Players in the O.J. Simpson Trial
item.description:
On the night of June 12, 1994, Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were brutally murdered in Los Angeles. The killings have remained unsolved for more than three decades, and have occupied a singular place in American pop culture, whetting the nation’s true-crime appetite and its obsession with violence and celebrity.

Books, television shows and an Oscar-winning documentary have cropped up in the decades since the 1995 trial, examining the fateful night and the actions of an entertainment and sports celebrity: O.J. Simpson.

Mr. Simpson was the Pro Football Hall of Famer turned commercial superstar who was charged and later acquitted in the murder of Ms. Brown Simpson, his ex-wife, and her friend Mr. Goldman.

No one has been criminally convicted in the double murder, although Mr. Simpson was found liable in a civil suit. Many of the people implicated or involved in the case have died, including Mr. Simpson in 2024.

A New York Times investigation published Sunday has added fresh intrigue to the “trial of the century.” It challenged the popular narrative about the case and raised questions about a possible accomplice who may have divulged information to investigators about the location of a murder weapon.

Here are some of the key players involved in the case, which captivated the country:

Revered by fans as “the Juice,” Mr. Simpson was a record-breaking N.F.L. running back and an American phenomenon. He was one of the first Black athletes to make inroads into corporate America, serving as a pitchman for the rental car giant Hertz and as an actor in multiple movies, including the comedy “Naked Gun” and its sequel. Despite mounting evidence against him, Mr. Simpson was acquitted of the murders.

The ex-wife and mother of two children with Mr. Simpson, Ms. Brown Simpson was stabbed repeatedly at her condominium in the Brentwood neighborhood of Los Angeles. In 1977, she met Mr. Simpson as an 18-year-old working at a Beverly Hills nightclub. Mr. Simpson, who was married at the time, began an affair with Ms. Brown. The two married in 1985 and divorced in 1992. Allegations of domestic violence by Mr. Simpson continued through their marriage and until her death.

Mr. Goldman was a waiter and friend of Ms. Simpson Brown. He had returned a personal item to Ms. Simpson Brown’s residence on the night of the crime and was found with a fatal knife wound.

A former professional football player and friend of Mr. Simpson. Mr. Cowlings drove Mr. Simpson in his white Ford Bronco on a Los Angeles freeway as a phalanx of police cruisers trailed behind. Inside the cab, Mr. Simpson oscillated between thoughts of suicide and of turning himself into the police. The televised slow-speed chase gripped the nation and was broadcast at Madison Square Garden, as the New York Knicks faced the Houston Rockets in the N. B. A. finals.

The lead prosecutor for the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office in the trial against Mr. Simpson, Ms. Clark resigned in disgrace after losing the case. The public has long scrutinized how the case against Mr. Simpson was lost, given the evidence. Investigators found Mr. Simpson’s blood and hair at the crime scene, as well as footprints that matched the size and model of his Bruno Magli shoes. They also discovered a glove at Mr. Simpson’s home, with the blood from both victims on it.

The second disgraced member of the prosecution team, Mr. Darden has been portrayed in documentaries as having been goaded into creating the trial’s most dramatic moment: when Mr. Simpson tried on the two bloodied gloves in court, before a jury. Ms. Clark was against the plan. The gloves did not fit.

Mr. Cochran was the defense team’s lead lawyer, known for his flamboyant style and verbal panache. In his closing arguments, he hinged his remarks on the moment when Mr. Simpson failed to put on the recovered gloves, telling the jury, “If it doesn’t fit, you must acquit.”

Although Mr. Cochran, who died in 2005, was ultimately successful, his legal strategy was controversial. He cast the charges against Mr. Simpson as a case about race relations in Los Angeles. That turned the trial into a referendum on local law enforcement, which had lost public support after the beating of Rodney King.

item.title: June 17, 1994: Millions Watched Police Chase O.J. Simpson in a Bronco
item.description:
More than 30 years ago, millions of Americans were transfixed by a police pursuit in the Los Angeles metro area. The person of interest? O.J. Simpson, a former football player who was charged, arrested and acquitted in the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

On June 17, 1994, Mr. Simpson refused to turn himself in to the local authorities, who accused him of killing Nicole Brown Simpson, his ex-wife, and her friend Ronald Goldman. He was declared a fugitive, and the police chased him in a white Ford Bronco driven by Al Cowlings, his close friend and a former football teammate.

The famous police chase prompted a media frenzy. News channels provided live coverage as Mr. Cowlings drove at a glacial pace for more than 50 miles.

It was the beginning of people’s fascination with Mr. Simpson’s case, which “marked a new chapter in electronic journalism.” And now, a new investigation by The New York Times indicates that an accomplice may have helped him to clean up his tracks and facilitated a potential escape at the end of the car chase.

Here are some highlights of the pursuit and what led to it.

On June 12, five days before the chase, Ms. Brown Simpson and Mr. Goldman were found slashed to death at the steps of her Los Angeles townhouse. She had just ended her efforts to rekindle her relationship with Mr. Simpson. Mr. Simpson’s blood, hair and footprints were found at the crime scene.

In the early morning of June 17, 1994, the Los Angeles Police Department informed Mr. Simpson’s lawyer that he would be charged in the murders and had to surrender by 11 a.m. Mr. Simpson delayed his arrival and told his lawyer, Robert Shapiro, that he needed to make arrangements with his family before he turned himself in.

When Mr. Simpson did not arrive in time, police officers were sent to a house in the San Fernando Valley where he was with Mr. Shapiro. A psychiatrist went to tell Mr. Simpson that the police had arrived, and that’s when “we discovered for the first time that O.J. was not present,” Mr. Shapiro said. Also missing was Mr. Simpson’s friend Mr. Cowlings.

The local authorities issued a message alerting officers and news agencies of Mr. Simpson’s escape and asked them to be on the lookout for a two-door white Ford Bronco.

In the evening, a young couple on a camping trip called the California Highway Patrol to report that they had seen the vehicle. Then, moments later, a Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Deputy saw the car heading north on Interstate 5.

Mr. Cowlings drove the vehicle at speeds ranging from 20 to 50 miles per hour for two hours. Dozens of officers following behind made no effort to pull the vehicle over because Mr. Cowlings had called 911 from the Bronco and told dispatchers that Mr. Simpson was threatening suicide and was holding a gun against his head.

Millions of Americans watched the pursuit live on television as news helicopters followed the vehicle.

Eventually the chase ended when Mr. Cowlings drove back to Mr. Simpson’s home in the Brentwood section of Los Angeles, where he was arrested.

A Times investigation published on Sunday revealed that there might have been an accomplice who helped Mr. Simpson cover up the murders and might have been trying to help him evade the police.

That accomplice, revealed to be a dead mobster named Joseph Ippolito, had escaped prison and was living in the Los Angeles area at the time that Ms. Brown Simpson and Mr. Goldman were killed.

Mr. Ippolito’s brother Sam Ippolito heard his sibling say that he had been “helping” Mr. Simpson. On the night of the murders, Mr. Ippolito left an apartment where he was staying and returned carrying a bag with a heavy object inside and appeared to have blood on his hands, Sam Ippolito said.

On a podcast last year, the rapper Fat Joe told a seemingly random story about a friend named “Joe” and Mr. Simpson. The rapper said that his friend Joey confided to him that when Mr. Cowlings and Mr. Simpson were in the Bronco chase, Joey had been at an airport, waiting with a private jet to help them escape.

Investigators did find a travel bag with a passport and a disguise kit inside the Bronco.

item.title: Trump Defends Plans to Ease Russia Sanctions and Hints at a Hostage Deal
item.description:
President Trump, defending his decision to ease tariffs and other sanctions against Russia, said on Sunday that he was making “great progress” in a peace deal with the Kremlin and suggested for the first time that the process included “hostage negotiations.”

He did not specify whose release he was seeking. But the only American now categorized by the State Department as “wrongfully detained” in Russia is Stephen Hubbard, a Michigan teacher who was seized from his home in Ukraine just months after Russia invaded that country in February 2022 and was charged with being a mercenary. He was sentenced to more than six years in a penal colony, on charges that the United States has said are fabricated.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media, an apparent reference to his move late on Friday to neutralize the sanctions resolution that he had signed only a few weeks earlier. “I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

Until Sunday, Mr. Trump had said little about the remarkable, rapid-fire steps he has taken over the past 10 days to side with the Russians in a conflict that has now gone on longer than World War I. Those steps amount to the reversal of nearly five years of sanctions following President Vladimir V. Putin’s decision to invade Ukraine.

In that time period Mr. Trump has announced that the United States will buy diesel fuel from Russia — though the announced purchases are far too small to have a significant effect on prices, despite Mr. Trump’s claims — and that he will waive imposing tariffs on Russia under a newly signed law named for its chief proponent, Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died in July.

Both decisions have been criticized by U.S. lawmakers, including fellow Republicans. Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, who was appointed to her brother’s seat and is now running for a full term, gently disagreed on Saturday with Mr. Trump’s decision on the sanctions law, saying that she “would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down.”

The breach with Ukraine has been sudden and perhaps irreparable.

Mr. Trump has declared publicly that Ukraine needs a new leader, the first time he has called for replacing Volodymyr Zelensky, the country’s president, with whom Mr. Trump has had a contentious relationship. And he and other administration officials have declined to explain whether they deliberately cut off intelligence warnings to Ukraine about incoming missile and drone attacks, or throttled the speed of data to the country from Starlink, Elon Musk’s critical satellite network, or its military cousin, called Starshield.

Taken together, those steps amount to a major reversal in U.S. strategy, after more than four years in which, to varying degrees, the United States has sided with Ukraine as the victim of Russian aggression.

And while Mr. Trump has episodically tacked toward Mr. Putin, for whom he has often expressed admiration, the United States has largely let intelligence assistance flow and continued to sell arms to Ukraine through the Europeans, who are paying for the deliveries.

But Mr. Trump and his two leading negotiators — Steve Witkoff, his special envoy, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law, who holds unofficial status as the president’s personal negotiator — have been trying a new approach. They have scrapped the administration’s previous insistence that business deals with Russia would come only after a peace accord was struck. Now they have announced the diesel deal, and they are trying to put together a purchase of Lukoil, one of Russia’s biggest energy companies, as an early confidence-building measure to assure Mr. Putin that they are about to uncork a series of lucrative projects.

Mr. Trump on Sunday accused Mr. Zelensky of targeting diesel refineries in Russia “knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.”

It is the opposite of the position he has taken in defending the blockade on Iranian oil shipments, in which he has said Americans are paying a necessary price to ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon. (Russia already has the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, and at various points in the Ukraine war, Mr. Putin has hinted that it may be used.)

In his social media post, Mr. Trump praised Russia for “sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World,” and he accused Mr. Zelensky of ingratitude. “Zelensky doesn’t care, and frankly, with all the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

Mr. Zelensky, for his part, has lamented Mr. Trump’s decisions as “weak” — a word he knows will inflame the president — and accused the president of pressuring Ukraine to relent to Russia.

item.title: Talarico Kicks Off Campaign Tour of Texas as Senate Election Looms
item.description:
James Talarico, the Democratic nominee running for the Senate in Texas against Ken Paxton, kicked off a 21-stop tour on Sunday that will take him across the state until the day before the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Mr. Talarico started his tour at an amphitheater in Plano, a Dallas suburb in Collin County, where President Trump won by more than 11 percentage points in the 2024 election. The tour comes as polls have shown an increasingly close race, though some polls indicate that Mr. Talarico has a slight lead over Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general. No Democrat has won a statewide election in Texas since 1994.

Mr. Talarico’s trek around Texas has been called the Clear Eyes Full Hearts Tour, a reference to the TV series “Friday Night Lights.”

The show chronicles a fictional Texas high school football team with the signature rallying cry of “Clear eyes, full hearts, can’t lose.” Three actors from the show appeared in a campaign video that Mr. Talarico posted on Sunday: Connie Britton, Jesse Plemons and Adrianne Palicki.

In a speech that lasted about 25 minutes, Mr. Talarico said that he liked the motto from “Friday Night Lights” because it emphasized the importance of closing out the campaign strong.

“We have to execute,” Mr. Talarico said. “We have to leave it all on the field. We have to win. Our fellow Texans are counting on us.”

The rally drew dozens of people who said they were attending their first campaign event for Mr. Talarico.

Tim Beahmer, 38, of Plano, said that while the rally on Sunday was his first event for Mr. Talarico, he had been following him for months. Mr. Beahmer said that one reason he wanted to support Mr. Talarico was because he thought the Senate candidate had not engaged much in culture wars.

“He just wants to put that aside and focus on the things that’ll actually help everybody,” Mr. Beahmer said.

Karen Malone, 67, of McKinney, said that the event on Sunday was her second time seeing Mr. Talarico. She said she voted for Mr. Trump in the 2016 election and had not planned to vote in the midterm elections until her children encouraged her to consider Mr. Talarico.

“I voted for Trump the first time, and then I said never again,” Ms. Malone said.

Mr. Talarico’s tour will wind through Texas, hitting Houston, Dallas and San Antonio as well as smaller cities like Lubbock in the Texas Panhandle and Galveston, a beach city southeast of Houston. The tour will end in Austin the day before the election.

Mr. Paxton began a dueling tour in North Texas on Saturday. He is expected to make more than 30 stops across the state before wrapping up the campaign in San Antonio on Nov. 2.

item.title: Larry David Mocks the D.S.A. Some Are Not Amused.
item.description:
The last time Larry David waded into politics with a satirical essay, it was to take aim at a very safe target in his liberal circles — President Trump.

Mr. David, who is known for his brand of anxious, observational comedy, mocked Bill Maher for dining with Mr. Trump at the White House in a guest essay published in The New York Times Opinion section last year headlined “My Dinner With Adolf,” in which he imagined dining with Hitler in 1939.

But Mr. David’s latest satire took aim at topics that are likely to be far more controversial within the coastal enclaves where his work is popular: the ascendant Democratic Socialists of America and its hostility toward Israel.

In a new essay published by Air Mail, the 79-year old comic channels the satirist Jonathan Swift and offers a dozen “modest proposals” for the manifesto of the socialist organization, whose actual proposals and guiding principles have been widely debated this year as several candidates aligned with the organization won primaries.

Mr. David’s suggestions start with ideas rooted in core planks of the movement, as he parodies proposals to abolish prisons and restrictions on immigration.

“In our Socialist America,” Mr. David writes, “everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes.”

“Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner,” he writes.

He rapidly progresses to more outlandish ideas, including national paid leave for the death of pets, mandating that employers provide cots for two siestas a day, allowing humans who identify as animals to “relieve themselves” wherever they wish and reparations that would enlist white people to serve as slaves for Black families.

Mr. David then aims his pen at one of the biggest fault lines dividing the Democratic Party, wading into the fraught debate over the line between opposition to Israel and antisemitism. Jews, he writes, will no longer be allowed to call themselves “the Chosen people” — a part of Jewish identity dating back millenniums — and will be known instead as “the Bagel People.”

“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” the proposal says. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty. We think the Bagel People will be very happy there.”

Best known for the hit TV shows “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” Mr. David has long been a prominent Democratic donor in Hollywood with an interest in political satire.

A national spokesperson for the D.S.A. declined to comment on Mr. David’s article. But online, some took umbrage at Mr. David’s satire of the democratic socialists. Matthew Gauna, a 29-year-old student in San Antonio who agrees with D.S.A. ideas but said he is not a member of the organization, replied online to a post comparing Mr. David to Mr. Maher by calling Mr. David “my problematic king,” with a wilted flower emoji.

“I don’t know if Larry is on top of his comedic game right now,” Mr. Gauna said in a phone interview.

Another post described the essay as “Larry David has a boomer crashout over Israel.”

Zack Wall, 35, of Columbus, Ohio, replied online to that post, writing, “Someone take the phone from gramps,” along with three crying-face emojis.

Mr. Wall said in a phone interview that Mr. David’s piece was an “utter disappointment.”

“Not so much that he was ragging on D.S.A. I don’t care about that part,” said Mr. Wall, who added that he identifies as a democratic socialist but is not a member of the D.S.A., with which he has some disagreements. “It was just so low-brow and unfunny. It can’t be the same person who wrote ‘Curb.’”

Many posts focused on Mr. David’s age while criticizing his views, and others described him as unfunny and racist.

“Maybe I’m just too young, but who is Larry David and why would any person alive care what he has to say?” said a user who identified themselves as DSA_Girly.

The Times sought to confirm the identities of the users who wrote these posts, but some declined to be interviewed or did not immediately respond to interview requests.

Mr. David, whose comedy has made him a millionaire many times over, did not mock the D.S.A.’s economic proposals, which include universal health care, raising the minimum wage and expanding public housing and child care. The movement’s focus on economic inequality is central to its appeal for many voters, who are struggling with higher costs and a dismal view of their financial future.

Mr. David seemed to anticipate the backlash his piece would provoke, daring his socialist targets to take the joke.

His last proposal mandates that any comedian who causes “emotional discomfort” be sent to be “re-programmed” to emerge with greater sensitivity.

And if that effort fails, Mr. David offers one final “modest” suggestion: “The repeat offender will be sent to Pitcairn Island to live with the Bagel People.”

item.title: The Frenzy Behind Getting an Initiative on the California Ballot
item.description:
Dederek Huff scanned the grassy hillside of Dolores Park in San Francisco one day this spring and saw dozens of people relaxing on picnic blankets and park benches.

To most people, it was an idyllic scene on a sunny day. To Mr. Huff, however, it was an opportunity to earn as much as $125 from each person in the park who would sign the stack of petitions under his arm.

“How y’all doing?” Mr. Huff asked as he approached a group of friends on a blanket. “Are you registered to vote?”

With his ease talking to strangers and his knack for reading a crowd, Mr. Huff used the same skills he said he had developed in a very different setting: selling party drugs on the Las Vegas Strip.

He had come to San Francisco because word had spread that campaigns were paying big money to place measures on the November ballot. So much, in fact, that Mr. Huff said he found he could make more money dealing democracy than dope.

“This is better than drug money,” said Mr. Huff, who has had drug-related arrests in Nevada, records show.

Mr. Huff was part of a small army of petition circulators who fanned out to shopping centers and street corners this spring, becoming the main reason that the ballots sent to California voters this month are stuffed with statewide initiatives.

California’s direct democracy system began over a century ago as a populist reform meant to empower citizens and bypass the special interests that controlled the State Legislature. Over the years, though, ballot measures have morphed into a sprawling industry fueled by moneyed interests that spend whatever it takes to put their ideas before voters.

This year, campaigns had to collect nearly 900,000 valid signatures to qualify a measure for the November ballot. To hit that number, most initiative efforts had to hire companies that specialize in this slice of the political process. The firms, in turn, contracted with smaller companies that paid people like Mr. Huff for each verified signature.

A flurry of spending was set off in January when a health care workers union began circulating petitions to put the billionaire tax on the ballot. That prompted a coalition of billionaires to flood the marketplace with three countermeasures that could void the tax initiative if they were to receive more votes in November.

Campaigns paid as much as $15 per signature, drawing a raft of enterprising workers — and some alleged fraudsters — to take part in this political underworld. It turned into a bonanza for workers like Mr. Huff, who said he made $43,000 in three months.

“That’s the most money I’ve made in three months of my life,” said Mr. Huff, 38.

All told, California ballot measure campaigns spent $126.5 million on circulating petitions during the first half of the year, four times as much as they spent in the same period in 2024, the last regular election year, according to state campaign finance reports.

As the price per signature doubled in March, a Facebook group for petition circulators lit up with excitement. Commenters called it a legendary season and punctuated their posts with money bag emojis. They shared pictures of invoices for tens of thousands of dollars as they submitted heaps of petitions. Employers recruited circulators from other parts of the country, sometimes offering housing or transportation.

But reports of bad actors and concerns of fraud also permeated the group. Workers posted warnings about managers who didn’t pay them and people who stole signed petitions. Some veteran petitioners expressed fear that the high price for signatures this year was spurring scams.

Things become so frenzied that men in ski masks handed out $5 bills and slices of pizza to people who signed petitions in a San Francisco neighborhood known for drug addiction and homelessness. And last month, three people were criminally charged after they were accused of paying people to sign petitions using stolen identities on Skid Row in Los Angeles.

In one pocket of Southern California, an experienced circulator with the biblical-sounding name of Third Corinthians Walker tried to instill some order. He confronted petition circulators who gave misleading information to voters or offered illegal giveaways. Then he posted their photos on the Facebook group and cited the laws he contended they were violating.

“This was the most hectic season I ever been in, in 25 years,” said Mr. Walker, 46, who lives in Redlands, Calif., about 60 miles east of downtown Los Angeles.

A lot of what he saw fell short of criminal behavior but broke the unspoken code of signature gathering, Mr. Walker said.

There were petitioners who set up tables at 2 a.m. to claim the best spot at a shopping center hours before stores opened. The “turf jumpers” who encroached on spots that other petitioners had already claimed. The “runners” who roamed parking lots and approached people as they got out of their cars.

Mr. Walker grew up in Kansas City, Mo. By the time he was 21, his felony record of gun and drug charges made it difficult to find employment. Feeling desperate, Mr. Walker saw a newspaper ad for a job promising $100 a day and went to an orientation on circulating petitions.

Over time, the work took him to places that he might never have otherwise seen: Florida, Nebraska, Ohio and, eventually, California.

“I felt like it was a blessing from the Lord,” Mr. Walker said.

Now, he runs his petition business with his mother, Melba Walker. They share a home in Southern California where, during the busy season, stacks of petitions covered the coffee table.

Mr. Walker likes the autonomy that comes with his profession, the ability to set his own hours and choose where he spends his time. He said he varies his pitch depending on the politics of the region. When he petitioned in a conservative area this year, he often led with the anti-tax measures; in liberal neighborhoods, he tended to start with the billionaire tax.

Now that it’s the offseason for petitioners, Mr. Walker keeps busy by playing video games and making graphic designs with Christian themes. He is also helping his mother write a book about their experiences as signature gatherers.

In San Francisco, Alex Carpenter, 49, made his first foray into petitioning this year after work dried up on the Northern California cannabis farm where he had spent the last several years.

Signature gathering appealed to Mr. Carpenter’s liberal activist streak, so he set up a table on a bustling corner near Golden Gate Park. It was close to his favorite coffee shop and had a lamppost where he could do pull-ups during lulls in foot traffic. He scrawled “Tax Billionaire$?” on a piece of card stock and taped it to the side of his table.

Many of the petitions on his clipboards represented causes Mr. Carpenter believed in. He liked the proposals to tax billionaires to fund health care, extend a tax hike on high-income earners to fund education and raise sales taxes to fund Bay Area transit. He focused on getting signatures for those initiatives.

He said he was still able to make close to $200 an hour, even though he didn’t actively pursue signatures for the highest compensated proposals that were backed by billionaires. Still, Mr. Carpenter had petitions for those measures on his table, in case voters took the time to get to the bottom of his stack of clipboards.

“I’m trying to make a living,” he said. “I would love to see them make it to the polls and fail.”

Mr. Huff, the petition circulator who sought signatures from voters in Dolores Park, also has strong political views.

He is a conservative and considers himself a part of President Trump’s MAGA movement. He has had an interest in politics ever since he was a teenager growing up in Louisville, Ky., he said.

That didn’t stop him from trying to make as much cash as possible in San Francisco, one of the nation’s most Democratic cities and where Mr. Trump is deeply unpopular.

After he finished gathering signatures this spring, Mr. Huff returned home to Las Vegas, where he spent time with his family for several weeks and used some of his petition money to buy new furniture and get work done on his teeth.

Despite his conservative views, Mr. Huff said he would do petition work for any campaign that pays him. So when a friend offered him a job gathering signatures for liberal-backed initiatives in Colorado this summer, Mr. Huff packed his bags and went.

Then he heard that conservative interest groups were also paying for signatures in Colorado.

“‘Well, bro,’ I said, ‘You got to get me on both petitions,’” Mr. Huff recalled.

“If I’m going to Colorado, I need as much petitions in my hand as possible because, of course, I’m trying to make the most money.”

Jill Cowan contributed reporting from Los Angeles. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: At a Last-Hope Health Clinic, Desperation, Kindness and Fear for What’s Next
item.description:
The early morning caller to Dr. Sarah Hershman’s personal cellphone was a patient.

Dr. Hershman, who works at a public health clinic in Nampa, Idaho, isn’t supposed to give out her private number. But she has been sharing it with some patients who she knows have no other recourse, telling them, “You really need to be able to contact me.”

Sophia Perez, 28, whose family has no health insurance, spoke in a frightened voice. Her husband, John, had been welding, she told Dr. Hershman, when he felt a hot sting on his eyeball. Could it have been hit by a metal shard? They could not afford a visit to a hospital emergency room.

Dr. Hershman asked careful questions and slipped him into the clinic’s packed Saturday roster.

Full Circle Health, where Dr. Hershman practices family medicine, has long been a last-hope safety net in the American health system. It is one of 1,400 networks known as federally qualified health centers with thousands of sites that receive federal funds to care for patients regardless of their ability to pay.

Now their caseloads are growing, even as revenues are falling. With cuts to Medicaid mounting and the cost of Obamacare insurance plans soaring, the clinic’s doctors and counselors are going to new lengths to patch together care for people with complex medical issues who are underinsured and uninsured.

Dr. Hershman and her colleagues have been spending hours providing unpaid care, emailing advice, calling after hours. They forage for cheaper but sometimes less effective medicines and spend weeks adjusting doses to make them as effective as possible. They negotiate with specialists to accept patients and offer to perform the work-up exams and follow-ups themselves.

Idaho has been one of the most aggressive states to slash Medicaid rolls over the past few years, affecting patients as well as clinics like Full Circle’s, which rely heavily on those funds to stay solvent. Now pressures on patients as well as clinics are about to become even worse, not only in the state but also throughout the country.

As harvest season for sugar beets, onions and potatoes winds down here, two ominous events loom on the calendar.

The annual enrollment period for Your Health Idaho, the state’s Obamacare marketplace, began on Oct. 15, but the generous government subsidies that helped make plans affordable are no longer available because Congress declined to renew them. Like many people, Mrs. Perez, whose job at an orthodontist practice includes filing insurance claims for patients yet cannot wrangle health care for her husband and 2-year-old, found that even the cheapest plan was out of reach. “It was all so overwhelming,” she said with tears in her eyes during her half-hour lunch break.

And come January, many patients covered by Medicaid — whose incomes are well under the state’s limits — may lose coverage. On New Year’s Day, new work requirements for eligibility, enacted as part of President Trump’s sweeping domestic policy bill, begin across the country. Idaho’s rules are among the nation’s most stringent.

At 8 a.m., Debbie Lehnert, a community health worker at the clinic, replenished a filing cabinet drawer with patient stress busters for the day: Bubble wrap for popping and Little Debbie Swiss rolls, the primal ones with chocolate cake, cream filling and fudge coating.

Ms. Lehnert’s responsibilities include connecting distressed patients with emergency health coverage and support services.

For weeks, she and her peers in public health clinics across the state have been under a weighty new burden: The rapidly approaching Medicaid work rules. Community health workers have been convening regularly in videoconferences to puzzle through the rules, discussing patient hypotheticals that none of them can answer with certainty.

Starting in January, Idaho patients will have to show documentation that they have worked or volunteered at least 80 hours a month for the previous three months. (Most states will require one month.) Reauthorization for the program will double in frequency, from the traditional yearly review to every six months. The requirements are expected to eventually reduce Medicaid rolls nationwide by five million people, the Congressional Budget Office estimates.

One of Ms. Lehnert’s most urgent tasks right now is to alert patients. She dialed the next one on her bottomless list. The young man, who can’t get his diabetes under control, had qualified for Medicaid after he lost his job at the post office for using too many sick days. Now his reauthorization date coincides with the start of the new work rules.

“I just wanted to see where you are in that process, if there’s anything I can do to help with that?” Ms. Lehnert said, gently prodding. “January is just around the corner.”

Given the man’s bleak health, it is unlikely he will be able to produce three pay stubs in time. Ms. Lehnert said that with the clinic’s records about his chronic diabetes, they could collaborate to seek an initial medical exemption.

“My hope is that would give you time to focus on getting better and finding employment, so that the second determination in six months would be easier,” she said.

“OK, yeah,” he replied dully.

Ms. Lehnert suggested they meet to attack the paperwork together. Or do a three-way call with a state assistant. Or he could file online, where, studies show, procedural errors, such as computer mistakes and confusion over directions, are the biggest reasons for lost coverage.

“OK, yeah,” he said.

“So which would you like to choose?” she pressed.

He chose online.

After they hung up, Ms. Lehnert buried her head in her hands.

“I truly feel like this is a calling, and I won’t do anything else,” she said, giving her dark curls an emphatic shake. “But these days, I’ve never hated doing my job more.”

It was just after 6 p.m. on a Thursday, but the buzzy restaurant was already slammed with people waiting for tables. Amid the kitchen chaos, Oscar Casarez, 37, a line cook and a patient at the Nampa clinic, kept his head down, juggling grill times and rhythmically seasoning burgers, steaks and salmon.

Just over a year ago, Mr. Casarez, lightheaded and gasping, drove himself to a hospital in septic shock. He was placed in a medically induced coma. By the time he was discharged nearly four weeks later, his employer had replaced him, leaving him uninsured as well as unemployed.

To cover Mr. Casarez’s six-figure bill, the hospital helped him get emergency Medicaid, which carried him through countless clinic visits, scans, blood transfusions and medications as well as hospital stays each time his newly diagnosed severe ulcerative colitis flared up.

Yet he managed to secure line-cook shifts. In May, he was booted off Medicaid because he started earning too much.

He works at two restaurants; neither offers health insurance. But his health problems continue: He also has a blood clot in his liver.

To help, Dr. Amanda Aman, his primary care doctor at the Nampa clinic, has been coordinating with a local gastroenterologist so she can monitor him at the clinic for lower fees than the specialist would charge. Case managers at the clinic scrounged for less expensive medication. After determining that the only drug that quells his colitis attacks requires an out-of-pocket monthly cost of more than $14,000, they helped enroll him in a special program that will provide the drug free for a year.

Still, given his precarious health, Mr. Casarez knows he needs insurance. His only option is to buy a plan on the state’s Obamacare marketplace.

He will likely have to select the most bare-bones policy, which has monthly premiums of about $310 and a deductible of $10,000. The plan doesn’t even cover his gastroenterologist.

At most, when he works 10 straight days of double shifts (to get an entire weekend with his 9-year-old son), Mr. Casarez can earn $3,800 a month. Rent takes a $1,400 chunk; then there are utilities, car payments, gas, child support, food, toiletries.

It comes down to this, he said: He can pay bills and insurance by working overtime at two jobs, almost guaranteeing a slow, steady death march. Or he can work fewer hours and get on Medicaid but have no money for housing and bills.

“I feel like I’m damned if I do and damned if I don’t,” he said.

Late one afternoon, Dr. Ty Waters, the tattooed director of Full Circle’s Nampa South clinic, unfurled himself into a chair in Ms. Lehnert’s office. He mused sarcastically about getting teardrops tattooed down one cheekbone, prison gang style, to signal the fights he gets into on behalf of his patients. He would nickname the tattoos his “Medicaid tears.”

Recently, a manual laborer without insurance injured his leg but held off coming in for weeks, wary of racking up a flurry of the clinic’s income-adjusted fees. When at last he limped in, Dr. Waters, who suspected that the man had torn his anterior cruciate ligament, treated him free of charge, put him in a stabilizing brace so he could return to work and coordinated with an orthopedist who would see him without requiring an expensive M.R.I.

“Our patients are basically people who are already struggling, who lose coverage and then get penalized for asking for help,” Dr. Waters said.

Dr. Hershman, who teaches family medicine to residents at the clinic, poked her head into Ms. Lehnert’s office, rubbing her face wearily. Every week, she allows a battered woman to sit in a clinic room for as long as she needs because the woman feels safe there. Dr. Hershman bills only a few dollars for the visit. It’s hardly conventional health care, she said, “but it’s that nexus of what we can do to improve their social situation and, therefore, their health outcomes.”

Her eyes glistened. “I love my patients, and I want to show up every day and be the person that they need,” she said. “Because even though this job is hard, being them is so, so much harder.”

(Dr. Hershman knows personally what it’s like to face crushing medical debt: After being treated for cancer recently, she discovered that her insurance doesn’t cover fertility preservation procedures. In addition, she owes $450,000 for her medical education.)

Too many times, Dr. Hershman said, she has sat with deathly ill patients who are nonetheless consumed with worries about cost, anxious about burdening their survivors with medical bills.

She treated a 59-year-old tech writer with a chronic gastrointestinal bleed that had turned life-threatening: Normal hemoglobin levels for men range between 13.5 and 17.5; his was 3.5. Or, as she put it: “He literally had no blood in the tank. I don’t know how his brain was functioning.”

She felt strongly that he needed to be hospitalized in intensive care because he required emergency surgery and, likely, a stay of five days. Chatting him up about his adored grandbaby, she almost got him to agree.

But then he dug in and, however reluctantly, refused. Her notes from that visit read: “Pt. doesn’t want to be here because of financial situation. Working to get insurance with open enrollment but has limited means.”
