item.title: Ken Paxton Has Tried to Overturn Tight Elections. He’s in One of His Own.
item.description:
In the immediate aftermath of the 2020 election, President Trump’s allies searched for a Republican state attorney general willing to back a last-ditch legal effort to challenge the results.

They found their man in Texas: Ken Paxton.

“No one had the courage or the clarity of legal understanding to do it,” Aaron Reitz, a top deputy to Mr. Paxton at the time, said in an interview. “Paxton and I were adamant that something needed to be done.”

The suit quickly failed at the U.S. Supreme Court, which found Texas had no standing to try to invalidate votes cast in another state. But it firmly established Mr. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, as a partisan fighter willing to wield the power of his office to aid Republicans, attack Democrats and challenge election results. It made him a conservative star and helped him secure Mr. Trump’s critical endorsement, propelling Mr. Paxton forward as the party’s nominee this year for U.S. Senate in Texas.

Early voting starts on Monday.

Since 2020, Mr. Paxton has continued to use his office to intervene in election disputes and pursue political opponents. Mr. Paxton has sued the former congressman Beto O’Rourke, tried to shut down a Latino voter registration group, opposed the counting of provisional ballots in Houston and unsuccessfully tried to criminally indict a sitting county election administrator.

Now, as he is locked in an extremely close contest against James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, Mr. Paxton’s record of election-related legal challenges and partisan legal actions has raised the question of how he would respond, in his capacity as attorney general and as a candidate, if he were to lose in November.

The Texas Senate race appears to have all the makings for a potential post-election legal fight by Mr. Paxton, should he lose. The contest is especially important to Republicans, who risk losing a statewide race for the first time in three decades and whose control of the U.S. Senate could hinge on the outcome. Current polls show Mr. Talarico with an edge in a tightening race.

“We have to win,” Mr. Paxton said at a rally hosted by President Trump in San Antonio this month.

Mr. Paxton, now in his third term as attorney general, has pushed to expand the powers of his office to prosecute criminal violations of Texas election law. Those efforts led to a clash with the state’s highest criminal court, made up of all Republican judges, which ruled that he lacked the authority under the state Constitution to independently prosecute election crimes.

After that loss, Mr. Paxton campaigned against the judges who ruled against him and were up for re-election, helping to oust them in a Republican primary in 2024. The next year, Republicans in the Texas Legislature passed a new law, Senate Bill 12, granting Mr. Paxton the authority to prosecute election crimes. But he has yet to test its constitutionality, and legal experts have said courts may again stymie Mr. Paxton if he tries.

His campaign defended his record.

“Ken Paxton has never apologized for enforcing Texas election law, and he never will,” Mr. Paxton’s campaign spokeswoman, Madison Cercy, said. “When elections are run fairly and the law is followed, every Texan wins.”

The attorney general’s office could also play a role, post-election, in investigating allegations of criminal conduct, or in securing election materials if asked by the secretary of state, who was appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican. The examination of the election materials would be directed by a state court.

Elections experts and voting security advocates said they worried that election challenges could be made in Texas, but they did not believe such challenges would be effective.

“The power he has under Texas law to enforce those criminal laws is quite limited,” said David Froomkin, a law professor at the University of Houston.

David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research in Washington, D.C., said that while the election could “potentially be a very volatile situation,” he was confident the courts and election officials in Texas were “going to hold firm.”

Mr. Abbott is tasked with certifying election results under state law, except in his own race and the lieutenant governor’s race, when the final canvass is done by the Legislature.

The role of the governor and Legislature in this process is ceremonial, election experts said, though he or the Legislature could face pressure to delay certification. This year, Mr. Abbott named Nate Schatzline, a hard-right former state representative who has questioned the 2020 election results, to be a senior adviser on elections.

Election challenges are permitted under Texas law. But Texas Republicans have, in recent years, challenged election results even when the outcome appeared clear.

In Harris County, which includes Houston, Republicans contested losses in more than a dozen races in 2022 — including one that the Democrat won by 15 points. Republicans cited what they said were problems at the polls. A court ordered a new election in only one case, a local judicial race.

Mr. Paxton also intervened on Election Day in 2022 to stop the counting of provisional ballots cast at locations in Harris County that had been kept open an extra hour. He sought to have the votes discarded. The Texas Supreme Court ruled against Mr. Paxton, ordering them to be counted — but left the possibility of further litigation open should the ballots cast during the extended voting hour swing any results. (They didn’t.)

Even within his own office, Mr. Paxton’s 2020 election challenge in support of Mr. Trump appeared to be contentious.

The solicitor general at the time, Kyle Hawkins, did not sign the Supreme Court filing, which Mr. Paxton signed himself along with Kurt Olsen, a lawyer who helped craft the unusual lawsuit that tried to challenge the election.

“Ken Paxton showed a tremendous amount of courage to take this on,” Mr. Olsen said in an interview this month.

Mr. Paxton, along with Mr. Reitz, his deputy for legal strategy, then brought the case to other Republican attorneys general to get them to file a supporting brief, Mr. Reitz said in the interview. Seventeen attorneys general signed on.

“It was a moment of character-revealing pressure,” Mr. Reitz said.

The Supreme Court quickly turned them all down.

Still, Mr. Paxton stood by his election challenge at a rally with Mr. Trump in Washington on Jan. 6, 2021. “If you look at what Georgia did, they capitulated, they consented,” Mr. Paxton told the crowd, referring to the state’s rapid certifications of its results. “We kept fighting in Texas.”

Mr. Olsen, who previously served as an elections czar for the White House, now works for the Justice Department. He recently stepped down from a high-profile elections investigation.

Mr. Reitz is now the top federal prosecutor in the Southern District of Texas, which includes Houston. He said in the interview that he would “muster all of my legal and law enforcement troops to ensure that federal law is upheld” in the 2026 election. But, he added, elections are primarily a state matter.

Since 2020, Mr. Paxton has announced dozens of election-related actions, including investigations and lawsuits.

Mr. Paxton tried in 2021 to prosecute Dana DeBeauvoir, who ran elections in Travis County, which includes Austin, on a charge of obstructing a poll observer in violation of Texas law. A grand jury declined to indict. In an interview, Ms. DeBeauvoir urged vigilance. “We’re at high alert,” she said. She added, “Let’s not let scare tactics work.”

In 2024, Mr. Paxton opened an investigation into Jolt Initiative, claiming the organization, which focuses on registering young Latino voters, had been illegally registering unauthorized migrants. The group sued, and a federal judge in Austin blocked his investigation, ruling the attorney general had acted in “bad faith.”

“Defendant could not offer any plausible proof,” the judge, Robert Pitman, wrote.

The suit had a significant financial impact, said Jackie Bastard, Jolt’s executive director, forcing it to cut its staff to five people from 35. The group has been able to register voters this year, Ms. Bastard said, but not at the same scale.

Then last fall, Mr. Paxton sued Mr. O’Rourke, the former Democratic congressman, and his voter registration group, claiming potential fund-raising violations. An all-Republican appeals court sided with Mr. O’Rourke. (The Texas Supreme Court, whose nine members are also all Republicans, declined to intervene.)

But as with Jolt, the case cost Mr. O’Rourke’s group time and more than $400,000, and, had it continued, could have bankrupted the organization, Mr. O’Rourke said at the time.

“We have seen Paxton try to use the power of the office to promote his political goals and the goals of his allies,” said Mimi Marziani, a lawyer and the former president of the Texas Civil Rights Project who represented Mr. O’Rourke.

“What I will say, which gives me a lot of hope,” she added, “is that by and large he has not been successful in the courts.”

A dispute over the election could end up before the Texas Supreme Court. The court’s newest member is Mr. Hawkins, the former solicitor general who did not sign on to Mr. Paxton’s election challenge in 2020.

item.title: Republicans in Ohio Are Worried About Turnout. Here’s What They’re Doing About it.
item.description:
Just two volunteers showed up on a recent weekday at a Republican Party campaign office near Cleveland that in 2024 was brimming with activity every night.

One of the two, Tanya Karabanovs, 54, sat among stacks of untouched yard signs and brainstormed new ways to convince her neighbors to vote for Republican candidates such as Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed in 2025 to finish the term of Vice President JD Vance. Her most recent idea: stuffing chocolate bars into goodie bags with leftover campaign literature.

“This is really a weird cycle,” said Ms. Karabanovs, who recalled at least 30 volunteers packing into the office each day in 2024. “There’s no way to feel confident about any of the races, honestly.”

Many of the Republican volunteers trying to keep Ohio’s Senate seat red started the summer making the case that, despite rising prices, Mr. Husted was better suited to fix the economy than his Democratic challenger, the former senator Sherrod Brown. But when it became clear that the message wasn’t landing, they began to pivot.

Some, like Ms. Karabanovs, got creative. The political PAC for Americans for Prosperity, a prominent conservative advocacy group that deploys thousands of door-knockers across the state, switched its script to the threat of socialism — and organizers quickly noticed a difference.

“I wouldn’t like that,” said Nikki Cvetkovic, 77, after opening her door in a working-class suburb of Youngstown and inspecting a pamphlet with a picture of Brown next to the words, “SOCIALISM THREATENS YOUR FREEDOM.” She said she would cast her ballot for Mr. Husted.

Polls have shown Mr. Brown running ahead of Mr. Husted in one of the most closely watched races of this cycle. But many conservatives across the state believe they can pull off in the final two weeks what Republicans have done better than Democrats for the last 10 years: defy expectations on Election Day.

The modern-day Republican Party is built on upsets. Twice, polls showed Mr. Trump losing the presidential election only for him to triumph, cementing the MAGA movement’s staying power and underdog status. The question now is whether the G.O.P. can do it again, at a time when Mr. Trump is not on the ballot and his popularity is historically low.

The answer lies on the ground in unexpected battlegrounds, including Iowa and Ohio, which have swung to the right over the last decade but this year have shown signs of shifting back. In these states, as the Republican Party has struggled to defend Mr. Trump’s handling of inflation, the war with Iran and tariff policies, local campaigns and committees have leaned into depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left — a last-ditch gambit to persuade their voters not to stay home or break the other way.

In a historically expensive midterm cycle, the Republican Party apparatus has poured more money into Ohio’s Senate race than all but one other contest, spending more than $277 million as of Saturday, according to AdImpact. At least a third of that spending has gone toward negative advertisements about Mr. Brown, many of which depict him as part of the far-left wing of the Democratic Party.

At Mr. Trump’s rally in Youngstown on Monday, he called Mr. Brown the “candidate of the Marxists, the communists, the anti-American radicals who want to tear down America’s heritage.”

It may not be enough. Representative Max Miller, one of President Trump’s closest allies in the House who has been besieged by allegations of domestic violence against his young daughter and ex-wife, came out against the war in Iran on Wednesday night during a meet-and-greet at a pub in Parma, a union town south of Cleveland.

National Republicans have withdrawn campaign funds from Ohio’s First Congressional District, where they had hoped to unseat a Democrat.

And a Republican National Committee operative circulated an email this week with data from Ohio showing Democrats outperforming Republicans in early vote, absentee votes and ballot requests compared with 2022 and 2018, according to an email reviewed by The Times.

Democrats in Ohio remain optimistic about returning Mr. Brown to the Senate, mostly because of Mr. Trump’s low approval rating and the deteriorating economy. But they also have benefited from Mr. Husted’s struggle to introduce himself to voters since he took office 21 months ago.

A former lieutenant governor and member of the House known for his outward reserve, Mr. Husted has tethered himself for much of the year to Mr. Trump, but he has also spent significant time describing his biography, including his time as a college football player and his upbringing as the son of a local factory worker focused on bringing jobs to the state.

Republicans, including Mr. Husted, are bracing for narrow margins on Election Day.

“We have a tough race, there is no doubt about that,” Mr. Husted said at an event last week at a G.O.P. field office in Mahoning County, which sprawls across three units of a strip mall in a region that once powered the country’s steel industry. “Midterm elections are tough.”

Mr. Husted had drawn a full house to the outpost in the Youngstown area, with supporters crammed between a plaque celebrating the Second Amendment and boxes of pizza. The crowd cheered when he took the lectern. As he spoke, rows of people nodded along and held up their phones to snap pictures.

“Find someone you haven’t talked to in a while, call them,” Mr. Husted continued. “You tell them I told you to call and ask them to vote, tell them that you spent time with me.”

Sitting in a plastic chair and listening along was Doris Layfield, who works at the board of elections in Mahoning County. She said she had knocked on doors for Mr. Husted and that she had liked what he said in person.

“Honestly, it’s really kind of scary,” she said. “If he doesn’t win, I really do feel like we will be living under communist rule.”

Mr. Brown, who was defeated in 2024 after three terms in the Senate, lost Mahoning County for the first time that year. The margin was just 220 votes.

He is aware that his victory is far from assured in a state that Mr. Trump won by 11 percentage points the same year he was unseated. He also seems to know that Republican claims that he’s a radical could resonate among Ohio’s increasingly conservative voters. He cut one ad, for instance, that responded to attacks from his opponent and an Elon Musk-backed PAC regarding transgender issues.

Mostly, though, Mr. Brown is running on the same progressive populism that has defined his political career since the 1970s.

In speeches at union halls, Mr. Brown talks about how the economy is “rigged,” says Congress is controlled by insider trading and describes Mr. Husted as a “special interest guy in Washington” who is detached from working-class people. He has also targeted Mr. Husted for his support for investments in data centers while he served in state government.

Aware of the resonance of the issue in Ohio, Mr. Husted sponsored a bill that passed in the House last month that encourages states to make data centers pay for higher energy costs, though it would not compel them to do so.

Back in the Youngstown area, Donovan O’Neil, a senior adviser in Ohio for Americans for Prosperity’s political PAC, walked up to a house with an American flag hanging from its porch. Barb Delaney, 65, a part-time bookkeeper, answered.

“Are you planning to vote?” Mr. O’Neil asked.

“Oh hell yes,” said Ms. Delaney, who was wearing a Detroit Lions T-shirt. “For Sherrod.”

Mr. O’Neil was not ready to walk away. He said he’d like to ask Ms. Delaney, a self-identified Democrat, a follow-up question: “Are there concerns for you with the rise of socialism, the Democrat Socialists of America?”

There were some, she said. But Ms. Delaney was far more incensed this year about data centers, and she blamed Mr. Husted. Because of a nearby development, she said, her energy bill, which includes heat for her pool, had surged from $200 a month to almost $500 — by far the highest it had been in the 28 years she had lived in her current home.

“My electric bill is skyrocketing,” she said. “Nobody wants data centers around.”

Then, referring to Mr. Husted, she added: “I will not vote for that man. I would never.”

Mr. O’Neil listened, and after a few more attempts to engage her, he continued down the block.

It’s triage season.

With just over two weeks to go until the midterm elections, Republicans reeling in a sour national environment have begun pulling spending out of tough territory, essentially cutting their losses in some races in an effort to rescue others.

North Carolina appears to be out. Kansas is in. Some House incumbents in New Jersey and Iowa are now on their own, while others in places like Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are receiving fresh infusions of national cash.

But even as the battleground moves into redder territory, Republicans see some signs of hope.

Polls are tightening in three Senate races in which Democrats have enjoyed narrow but consistent polling leads: Texas, Ohio and Michigan. And, thanks to a cascade of outside money, Republicans have ample resources to keep hammering their opponents in those states and beyond. item.title: Vital Early Voting Period Begins in Texas
item.description:
The time has finally come: Texans can begin casting ballots on Monday, and their early votes will help determine whether a prospective Democratic revival nationwide will upend three decades of statewide Republican rule.

Most votes in Texas tend to be cast early, with 80 percent coming before Election Day in 2024 and about two-thirds in 2022, according to state election data. That means campaigns will be hustling to get their supporters to the polls from now until Oct. 30, when the state’s early voting period ends.

The candidates in the Senate race — Ken Paxton, the Republican, and James Talarico, the Democrat — have already begun statewide tours, and will be holding events around the state almost daily through Election Day.

On Monday night, the candidates are set to hold dueling rallies in Fort Worth, underscoring the importance of the city and surrounding Tarrant County. Mr. Paxton and his Republican supporters are looking to mobilize their voters in an area of the state where Democrats have been making inroads recently, while Mr. Talarico and his party see the county, a swingy area in recent elections, as crucial to any statewide victory.

But by now both candidate’s faces and voices have been seared into the eyes (and ears) of Texas, thanks to the more than half a billion dollars that have been spent on television advertising already. Much of the spending has come late in the race, and a huge portion of it has been financed by one man, Elon Musk, to benefit one candidate, Mr. Paxton.

Both Senate candidates are coming off rocky periods in their campaigns. Mr. Talarico was absent from the campaign trail for nine days because of what he has said was a “nasty case of the flu.” Mr. Paxton has faced a run of unflattering headlines, including one after a video showed him celebrating New Year’s Eve in 2024 at a Dubai high-rise with two fugitives and a woman who is not his wife — months before their divorce was announced publicly.

The Senate race isn’t the only hotly contested campaign on the ballot. Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, is hoping that he can win a record fourth term. But polls have shown that even Mr. Abbott — a prodigious fund-raiser and able campaigner — has been struggling amid the general sour mood of the electorate.

Unlike in previous races, Mr. Abbott has opted not to debate his Democratic opponent, Gina Hinojosa, an Austin state representative. Mr. Abbott agreed, in 2022, to a televised debate against Beto O’Rourke, a much better known opponent. (Mr. Abbott won that race by double digits.)

But the governor’s decision was in keeping with that of other Republicans in statewide races this year: None have agreed to debate their Democratic opponents. Some odd moments have resulted, like Mr. Talarico’s appearance at a CNN town hall, debating with Republican voters who are not Mr. Paxton, or Ms. Hinojosa’s staging a debate against an empty lectern in front of the governor’s mansion in Austin.

It once seemed as though the one debate that would take place would be between candidates for the statewide position of railroad commissioner, which helps regulate the oil and gas industry. The race has attracted lots of attention this year, after the hard-right anti-immigration Republican candidate, Bo French, posted racist attacks after seeing South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game. He had been slated to debate Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat, but said last week that the showdown would not happen.

item.title: That Huge Republican Cash Edge? It’s in Senate Races, Not House Races.
item.description:
Republicans have an enormous financial edge in this year’s midterms. But with two weeks until the election, it is now clear that their spending advantage is overwhelmingly playing out only in the advertising battle for the Senate — not the House.

In the seven Senate races that the Cook Political Report rated as tossups, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising by $947 million to $625 million. That is a breathtaking advantage of more than $320 million in the key races that could determine which party wins control of the Senate, according to a tally by AdImpact of ads that have been already been shown and future reservations.

It is a very different story in the House, though. Republicans still have an advertising advantage in the closest House races, but it is relatively narrow — just a $14 million edge across the 21 races rated as tossups.

There are a number of explanations for the discrepancy.

Senate races generally attract more money and attention than congressional contests. Elon Musk’s enormous spending on the Texas Senate race is also a factor: He gave nearly $170 million to super PACs backing Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee there — a huge injection of cash from one person.

But it is also appears to be an indication that both parties — and their donors — are viewing it as increasingly unlikely that Republicans will be able to hold onto their House majority. The battle to win control of the Senate, though, remains on a knife’s edge. Republican donors are accordingly spending big in key Senate races.

In six of the seven tossup Senate races, Republican ad spending is far outstripping Democrats’. The biggest gap is in Texas ($141 million), but there are chasms also in Ohio (nearly $90 million), Maine (nearly $32 million) and Michigan ($33 million).

Only in Kansas — where Republicans are engaged in a late rescue mission — is the spending even close. There, Democrats had an edge of less than $2 million.

In the House, there is not such a clear-cut edge for Republicans. Across the 21 tossup districts, Republicans are currently set to spend more on 10 seats while Democrats are set to spend more on 11.

It is worth noting that in recent years, Democrats have lapped Republicans in House spending. In President Trump’s first midterm election, in 2018, G.O.P. strategists spoke about being washed away in a “green wave” as much as a blue one.

“This cycle, that money won’t save them,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee. “Republicans have the money, the map and the message.”

Republicans do have a roughly $30 million spending edge in the dozen seats that are leaning Democratic — but Democrats have a narrow edge of less than $1 million in the 13 seats that are currently rated as leaning Republican.
